data.title: Surge in software patches likely behind recent tech outages, experts say
data.description:
WHILE the causes of recent disruptions to the way people work, access bank accounts and travel remain unclear, increased efforts to rapidly patch newly discovered vulnerabilities in the AI age are likely a major factor, according to cybersecurity experts and US officials.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking to reporters in Manila this week, said company patching efforts are, at times, “creating short-term disruption in the way the system works.”

Patches are software and operating system updates intended to fix security vulnerabilities found within a program or product.

A string of technology outages affecting airlines, workplaces and online banking has intensified concerns that organisations are struggling to keep pace with the flood of software vulnerabilities being uncovered and patched in the AI era.

Banking executives said that they were rushing to fix the patches after a technical outage disrupted online operations earlier this week.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told a House of Representatives Homeland Security Committee hearing on worldwide threats on Wednesday that there is so far no indication that the tech outages are related.

But Clayton said the speed and level of capability of computer systems are “increasing substantially,” so legacy computer systems and equipment that already were old are aging much more quickly.

The advent of easily accessible AI tools and large language models has supercharged the discovery of vulnerabilities in software.

Microsoft this month has addressed more than 1,200 software vulnerabilities, nearly 20 times higher than in the same month a year ago, according to cybersecurity firm Qualys.

“AI has made finding critical vulnerabilities fast and cheap, and the number of flaws that demand immediate patching has grown with it,” said Yuval Itzchakov, CTO and co-founder of autonomous offensive security company A Security.

“Emergency patches go into core infrastructure within hours, often without the full testing cycle, and they are intrusive by design: they change runtimes, kernels and network components that everything else depends on. That speed and scale of change is itself a source of failure,” Itzchakov said.

Josh Bressers, director of coordinated vulnerability disclosure at cybersecurity firm VulnCheck, said that in 2026 there have been 100,000 publicly disclosed vulnerabilities, tracked by industry as Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, or CVEs. Of those, Bressers said, 1,363 were known to have been exploited in the real world.

“Given tight resources for defenders, understanding which vulnerabilities need attention first is critical,” Bressers wrote in a LinkedIn post. “Not all vulnerabilities are created equal.”

Anne Neuberger, general partner at Andreessen Horowitz, said that AI is helping attackers find and weaponise vulnerabilities, but is a more “valuable friend” to those tasked with defending key computer networks.

“AI is enabling enterprises to find 10 times more vulnerabilities,” said Neuberger, who served as deputy national security adviser under former President Joe Biden and led incident response to serious national incidents. “And when patching at scale, some can cause problems.”

Bank vulnerabilities

At least one major bank was rushing to address a wave of recent patches and there is a lot of work needed, a source at the bank said, speaking on condition of anonymity.

Lenders had also received inquiries from the banking regulator, Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, after the outages, another source said. The US regulator was trying to assess the impact and also asked about increased customer communication, the source added.

The OCC did not immediately respond to a request seeking comment.

“The banks and everyone else have had a short-term goal on efficiency and cutting costs when it comes to AI, and that has built a technical deficit,” said John Cosgrove, head of Walden Advisory, an enterprise security and resilience advisory firm. “That might have not been a problem on its own, but AI is now introducing a speed and scale of changes that you can’t keep up with,” Cosgrove said.

Ronald Gestiehr, director of wealth management at Luttner Financial, said technology has made banking “incredibly convenient, and while occasional outages can be frustrating, I don’t believe the outages will have a significant impact on consumer confidence or change how most people manage their money.”

“Financial institutions have invested heavily in technology and security, and, unfortunately, occasional disruptions will happen,” Gestiehr said. “What matters most is how quickly those issues are identified, resolved and communicated to customers.” REUTERS

data.title: Singapore is winning the HQ race. Is it winning the leadership race?
data.description:
SINGAPORE now hosts about 1,030 foreign headquarters, up from roughly 770 in 2019. Over the same period, the resident professionals, managers and executives (PMEs) working in them grew by less than 8 per cent, from 12,700 to 13,700, as The Straits Times reported recently.

The explanation on offer is reassuring. A regional headquarters today, one adviser told the paper, is often “a leaner set-up focused on senior decision-making”, while operational roles move to cheaper markets.

That may well be true. The problem is that nobody measures it. Singapore counts its headquarters well. It does not yet count what they decide.

What the numbers miss

The PME figures also leave out foreign professionals, so headcount was never the right test of a headquarters. What matters is whether decision-making authority grew alongside the count. On that, the published figures are silent.

The Economic Strategy Review, published in June 2026, wants Singapore’s own companies to keep “headquarters, strategy and decision-making” functions here as they expand abroad, and foreign investors to make Singapore “a critical node” in their operations.

A headquarters, in the sense that counts for an economy, is where decisions are made. For a startup that re-domiciles here, that means where its chief executive and senior team sit.

Flipkart, founded in Bengaluru and serving customers across India, was incorporated in Singapore for 15 years before completing its move back to India in March 2026, ahead of a planned listing.

Throughout that time, Flipkart’s operations stayed in India alongside its executive leadership, while the Singapore headquarters focused on raising capital.

Grab offers a counter-example. Founded in Malaysia, the startup uses its Singapore headquarters as a control centre to manage localised teams across eight South-east Asian markets.

For a multinational’s regional headquarters, the test is narrower. In matrix organisations, few regional heads own every budget.

Even as global head offices hold ultimate control over bigger budgets, genuine regional headquarters can exert strategic influence and anchor a high-value ecosystem of professional services. For this, local leaders require sufficient autonomy.

Can the leaders here approve investment in the region, hire their own team and stop a project without needing a flight to the head office?

The Swiss mirror

Switzerland, where I am based, shows how control can move while the address stays.

Switzerland’s two federal technology universities, ETH in Zurich and EPFL in Lausanne, each produced a record number of new companies in 2025. But Swiss investors supplied at most about 13 per cent of later-stage capital for local startups that year, the Swiss Scale-Up Report 2026 found.

Growth money comes mostly from abroad.

Nexthink, an EPFL spin-off, is a Swiss success story. It still names Lausanne as one of its two headquarters. Its founder and chief executive, however, lives in the Boston area, and in October 2025, the company agreed to sell a majority stake to the American investor Vista Equity Partners.

On paper, Nexthink remains a Swiss-headquartered company. Where its biggest decisions are now taken is a different question.

That is also the risk Singapore faces: A company can maintain its official address in the country long after its true centre of decision-making has moved abroad.

When authority stays at home

In one executive search I handled, a company hired a Singapore-based leader for their understanding of the Asean market.

Yet headquarters, thousands of kilometres away, controlled the expansion budgets, assuming that what worked at home would work in the region.

The hire left for a direct competitor after 14 months, telling me that the lack of decision-making authority was the reason. The company had recruited local judgment but left it little room to act.

Retaining control overseas cost the company the local expertise it had recruited for its regional hub.

Singapore may get the leadership role, but does the authority move with it?

It can go the other way. In October 2026, Nike said the leadership team for a combined Asia-Pacific and Greater China region would be based in Singapore from fiscal year 2028, with some roles moving from its US headquarters.

Whether moves such as that bring real decision rights with them is exactly what Singapore should be tracking.

Closing the gap

Three changes would help.

First, measure authority as well as addresses. Singapore already counts its foreign headquarters and the resident PMEs in them. It could also survey whether those headquarters hold budget and hiring authority for the region, and publish the results in aggregate.

For startups that re-domicile, it could track where the chief executive and senior team are based.

Second, tie incentives to actual decision-making rights.

Today’s international headquarters award counts skilled jobs and local spending. Managing the group from Singapore is one qualifying activity among several, but it is not required.

As Singapore reviews its incentives for the era of the global minimum tax, awards could give weight to whether a regional chief executive or finance chief is a tax resident here and holds the regional budget.

Third, companies should move authority along with the address.

A startup that re-domiciles for capital or neutrality, while keeping every senior role elsewhere, has bought an address. A multinational that hires a regional leader here but signs off every budget at home has bought a title.

Businesses that put real decisions here, give regional leaders real budgets, and hire the next layer locally get what the address was meant to bring: proximity to regional customers, a deeper pool of talent and credibility with the investors who now concentrate their money here.

Singapore has already won the argument about where companies in this region want to be registered. The harder contest is about where they are run from.

To stay the region’s launchpad in 2027 and beyond, Singapore should count not only its headquarters, but also what they are allowed to decide.

The writer is the founder of Gunia Consulting, an advisory and executive search firm for organisation and leadership, with mandates in Europe and Asia, including Singapore. He is based in Zurich.

Views expressed here are his own. He used AI tools for research and editing before submitting the draft.

data.title: Asiaâs family offices cool to Anthropic IPO despite strong investor demand
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Anthropic’s initial public offering has reportedly attracted demand exceeding six times the shares on offer, but some Asia family offices are holding back, citing steep valuations and the prospect of better buying opportunities after the listing.

Despite the fanfare surrounding the landmark listing of the artificial intelligence firm, family offices and wealth advisers in Asia said that much of the company’s potential growth has already been priced in.

At the same time, geopolitical uncertainty and risks associated with the technology warrant caution, they noted.

Anthropic is targeting a valuation of about US$1.4 trillion in its IPO. It aims to issue 825 million shares.

The offering was scheduled to be priced on Wednesday (Nov 18) evening US time, or Thursday morning in Singapore. Anthropic’s shares are expected to begin trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday.

Cameron Harvey, CEO of Hong Kong-headquartered Landmark Family Office, said that sophisticated family offices are taking a selective approach rather than chasing day-one momentum.

For investors without existing positions, the risk-reward balance favours waiting for trading activity to settle, he noted. Recent IPO performance suggests that more attractive entry points could emerge after listing.

He added that investors should pay particular attention to post-listing discovery and the expiry of lock-up periods, which could release additional shares into the market.

Arnold Ho, head of trading at Moomoo Singapore, said that demand was being driven by major institutional commitments, including reported cornerstone investments from Nvidia and Altimeter Capital, alongside strong retail interest.

Existing backers are prioritised for allocations, with some reportedly offering pre-IPO shares at a 3 to 5 per cent premium, he said, adding that the day-one float will therefore be limited.

With a limited initial free float and elevated opening demand, there could be heightened volatility and wider bid-ask spreads as the market establishes a trading price, believes Ho.

“But strong subscription demand does not guarantee that the shares will trade above the IPO price,” he cautioned.

A comparable mega-listing was SpaceX, which listed in June this year.

Its offering was more than three times oversubscribed, with shares rising 19 per cent on the first day of trading. The equity fell below its listing price of US$135 about a month later on Jul 15. It closed at US$141.70 on Tuesday.

LN Sadani, founder and CEO of Singapore-based single family office Lensbridge Capital, said that Anthropic’s competitive advantage warrants closer scrutiny than Space X’s, given the latter’s established launch and satellite infrastructure.

He pointed to the potential for open-source models to erode pricing power, and to the AI firm’s own warnings about compute dependence, harmful model behaviour and legal or regulatory exposure as some reasons for staying cautious on Anthropic.

Value created in private markets 

For some family offices, the bigger concern is that investors buying into Anthropic’s IPO may be arriving after much of the company’s valuation gains have already been realised as a private company.

Singapore sovereign wealth fund GIC has been an investor since 2025, most recently co-leading its US$65 billion fundraising in May. GIC reportedly holds about 1 per cent of the firm after investing north of US$4.5 billion in it, according to reports.

Singapore investment company Temasek has also invested in Anthropic, as part of its focus on deep-tech innovation.

“The Anthropic IPO is a landmark for private markets as much as public ones,” said Grace Tang, CEO and managing director of Phillip Private Equity.

“Most of the value creation has already happened, while the company was private. Family offices that want the next Anthropic need to be in private growth equity before the IPO, not after.”

Sadani similarly views the listing as a potential liquidity milestone for patient capital, but noted that substantial growth expectations are already reflected in private valuations.

Lensbridge Capital, however, did not invest in the pre-IPO rounds for Anthropic, as it expects more attractive opportunities to invest in the company to emerge after listing.

Broader technology sector

The listing is also being watched for its effect on the wider technology market, following a difficult month for the sector.

James Ooi, chief market strategist at Tiger Brokers, said the IPO could be an important test of market appetite for AI companies.

Meanwhile, Harvey described Anthropic – as the first frontier-AI model developer to list publicly – as a bellwether for the sector, at a time when the market is repricing future earnings assumptions.

A public raise of about US$60 billion-plus, alongside a US$26 billion strategic placement, will absorb significant institutional capital, potentially creating rotational pressure across legacy software and mega-cap tech peers as allocators rebalance their AI exposure, he noted.

Moomoo’s Ho also expects some savvy investors with concentrated exposure to semiconductor or cloud stocks to also review their positions to free up capital for Anthropic.

“However, we would not assume that clients will hedge systematically, or that the IPO will necessarily cause a liquidity drain from those stocks.”

Kam Kah Ken, CEO and chief investment officer of single family office Wellco Capital, noted that he has seen an aggressive shift of capital from AI and semiconductors into non-AI themes in recent weeks.

He nevertheless remains bullish on the sector. “Compute power is the new oil, and hyperscalers are still committed to spend (many) billions on data centres,” he said.

Geopolitics and risk disclosures

Kam added that the bigger drain on liquidity will be regulation and geopolitics, which are unfolding alongside the broader IPO market.

He highlighted the uncertainty over US restrictions on advanced AI chips, particularly their implications for South-east Asia data centres serving Chinese customers.

“Close to home, our biggest open secret is how South-east Asia regional data centres powered with advanced Nvidia chips cater to large Chinese customers like Alibaba and ByteDance,” he said.

“All the new regional data-centre builds depend on the US restricting only physical chip ownership, and not remote access by the Chinese.”

This risk has become more pressing as Washington moves to tighten restrictions on remote access to advanced AI chips, raising uncertainty over the region’s AI infrastructure expansion.

Meanwhile, Anthropic’s own risk disclosures add another layer of uncertainty for prospective shareholders.

Ooi said the extensive disclosures may introduce a dimension of uncertainty that is difficult to capture in traditional financial models.

“Investors are being asked to assess not just an emerging business model, but (also) a technology whose long-term risks and implications remain hard to quantify.”

data.title: How should success of Singaporeâs IPO market be defined?
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Something is decidedly odd about celebrating the revival of Singapore’s initial public offering market when the majority of new listings in 2026 are trading below their offer prices, despite the Straits Times Index hitting numerous record highs this year.

As at early November, seven of the 12 new listings on the Singapore Exchange (SGX) were underwater.

Yet, the industry continues to trumpet the number of listings, the amount of capital raised and the supposed resurgence of interest in Singapore stocks.

So, how exactly should IPO success be measured?

Is it a success when shares are fully or oversubscribed, in which case companies raise their targeted capital and intermediaries collect their fees?

Is it when investment bankers are happy and the exchange can chalk up another listing?

Or should success be evaluated from the viewpoint of investors?

An uncomfortable question follows: Is the local IPO market structured primarily for major shareholders and early investors to cash out and intermediaries to earn their fees – at the expense of the investing public?

Consider the incentives involved.

Issuers and vendors naturally want the highest possible prices for their shares.

Investment bankers and issue managers are incentivised to complete transactions as quickly as possible, since fees are generally linked to the size and successful execution of offerings.

Investors, meanwhile, want precisely the opposite – to buy shares at reasonable valuations (read: low prices) that offer scope for meaningful capital appreciation.

Of course, there is nothing inherently wrong or improper about these competing objectives, because that is how capital markets operate.

But when the overwhelming majority of new listings flop as they have this year – and many, very quickly after their debut – surely, it is reasonable to question whether the balance has tilted too far towards the sellers.

Perhaps, those responsible for bringing companies to market should have skin in the game after the IPO bell rings.

Stated differently: Is there any way to ensure part of an issue manager’s remuneration is dependent on post-listing performance over, say, six to 12 months?

Mechanics aside, the underlying principle is accountability.

A publicly accessible scorecard tracking the performance of IPOs, sorted by issue managers, over different periods – six months, one year, three years and so on – would support this.

Such information would allow investors to distinguish between intermediaries with a consistent record of bringing reasonably priced companies to market, and those whose offerings regularly disappoint.

Importantly, these questions come at a time when the IPO process is being streamlined, with SGX RegCo assuming prospectus review functions from 2027.

Efforts to reduce unnecessary regulatory friction are commendable, but making it easier and faster for companies to list should not become an end in itself.

The success of the ongoing Equity Market Development Programme should not be measured by the number of IPOs attracted to SGX, because investor confidence cannot be manufactured through promotional campaigns, fancy listing ceremonies and impressive subscription rates.

It should be earned through credible, quality companies, fair pricing and satisfactory long-term returns.

After all, what is the point of reviving Singapore’s IPO market if the principal beneficiaries are everyone except the investors who finance it?

data.title: Anthropic IPO to mint thousands ofÂ millionaires
data.description:
[NEW YORK] Anthropic’s initial public offering is poised to create thousands of paper millionaires among current and former employees, in what could rank among the largest employee wealth windfalls in Silicon Valley history.

The offering is expected to unleash a wave of new wealth across the AI sector, rewarding everyone from early researchers and engineers to administrative staff who received stock grants as the Claude maker raced from startup to one of the world’s most valuable companies.

The IPO filing shows the amount of wealth embedded in employee stock awards, but not how that wealth is distributed among workers. As a result, outside estimates vary widely.

Hill, a San Francisco marketplace for private-company shares, estimates 598 non-founder employees will hold at least US$100 million in equity after the initial public offering, which is slated to open on the Nasdaq on Thursday at US$83 a share, above its initial target range that would value the company at up to US$1.4 trillion, according to a person familiar with the information.

Private-markets research firm Sacra estimates that roughly 2,800 current and former Anthropic employees could hold at least US$1 million of pretax vested equity at a US$1.35 trillion valuation, the middle of the price range.

The firms say their estimates are model-based and use public information. Reuters could not independently verify the estimates, which reflect factors including vesting periods, exercises, tender transactions, option awards, restricted stock units, award timing, headcount and employee retention rates. The filing does not disclose sums due individuals.

But the wealth potentially shared by employees is vast. Anthropic option holders were sitting on US$119 billion of paper gains as of Sep 30, at a weighted average exercise price of US$2.91 per share, the company disclosed. About US$73 billion of that amount had vested through service and could be exercised immediately.

Anthropic did not respond to a comment request on the estimates.

“The idea of equity appreciating to an amount that is life-changing is something that people strive for,” Hill CEO Andrew Benson said. “It doesn’t get better than this.”

Equity at entry level

Workers who joined the firm when it started five years ago — even in administrative positions and entry-level jobs — could be sitting on life-changing wealth, reflecting their holdings of stock options that carry exercise prices of less than US$1.

Options granted through 2023 and still outstanding at the end of that year carried an average exercise price of 52 cents, the filing shows.

At SpaceX, which was founded in 2002 and went public in June in a record-busting IPO, many of the employees who became millionaires had worked there for more than a decade.

“Early employees who started in a very junior role should have actually a better financial outcome than somebody who joined in a very senior role right before the IPO,” Benson said, referring to Anthropic.

Non-founder Anthropic employees can sell up to 10 per cent of their holdings on the first trading day, and up to another 35 per cent after fiscal 2026 earnings.

Early hires reap rewards

Founded in 2021, the Claude maker expanded its workforce rapidly alongside the AI boom, growing to about 5,300 employees as of Sep 30 from roughly 940 at the end of 2024. As it hired aggressively, the company used stock-based compensation as a key recruiting tool.

A May 2024 job posting for an administrative business partner role shows how the benefits of Anthropic’s stock awards extended beyond AI researchers and engineers.

The position, which involved scheduling and managing calendars for company leaders, coordinating conference logistics and handling expense claims and reimbursements, paid an annual salary of US$140,000 to US$190,000.

The posting added that equity would be “a major component of the total compensation” beyond the salary, indicating that administrative and support staff were also eligible for stock awards alongside cash pay.

That year, Anthropic said it granted employees options at an average exercise price of US$1.30 per share.

“And as we know from several anecdotes after the SpaceX IPO, this is often enough to help people down the organization chart do quite well in IPO,” said Marcelo Ballve, head of research at Sacra.

Anthropic granted CFO Krishna Rao 14 million stock options in 2024, also with a US$1.30 exercise price, according to the filing. At the IPO price range, those options would carry roughly US$1 billion in gross intrinsic value, before exercise costs and taxes.

Ballve said that equity awards for administrative, support and entry-level roles are not uncommon at venture capital-backed companies. Historically, though, many companies phased out equity grants at hiring for these roles as they scaled up and salaries became more competitive, moving to performance- and tenure-based grants instead.

After Anthropic goes public, the company will likely reserve upfront equity grants solely for recruiting top talent, he said. REUTERS

data.title: Federal Reserve policymakers concerned about financial system risks, minutes show
data.description:
[NEW YORK] Financial stability risks tied to aggressive artificial intelligence investment and elevated asset prices are on the US central bank’s radar, the minutes from the Federal Reserve’s policy meeting last month showed on Wednesday (Nov 18).

The concern was raised as part of a broad review of financial risks by Fed policymakers and central bank staff at the Oct 27-28 policy meeting.

That gathering saw officials hold interest rates steady despite ongoing worries about high and persistent levels of inflation. However, “almost all” policymakers agreed that further hikes would be needed if the economy evolved as they expected, the minutes showed.

“The staff judged that current vulnerabilities could amplify shocks somewhat more than usual, with elevated asset valuations and leverage at hedge funds representing the most salient vulnerabilities, while strong bank and household balance sheets provided an important buffer against more severe outcomes,” the minutes said.

Policymakers expressed concern that huge levels of investment in AI technology could lead to trouble and create broader problems for both the financial system and economy.

“Almost all participants commented on risks associated with a scenario in which the returns on AI investment turned out to be disappointing to investors,” the minutes said.

“Most participants observed that AI-related debt had grown rapidly and that much of this growth had taken place through complex and opaque financing structures,” while “a few” of the unnamed Fed officials were concerned that AI exposure was being concentrated in a “small number” of companies.

Fed officials also cast an anxious eye toward hedge funds.

“Most participants highlighted hedge fund leverage or limited dealer intermediation capacity as potential channels of amplification during periods of market stress,” the minutes said.

Fed staff described the financial system as “resilient,” with banks having ample access to cash, according to the minutes. But some policymakers worried that “banking system vulnerabilities could emerge rapidly even after seemingly reassuring initial assessments.”

Some were also worried the Fed‘s data on the banking system may miss the full range of exposure some financial firms have.

Building resilience

Financial markets have been under stress in recent weeks amid questions about the future of AI and how the buildout of the technology has increasingly come to rely on debt. Past periods of financial trouble have been frequently associated with excessive borrowing, and some of those crises have driven the Fed to intervene to stabilise markets.

The latest minutes also showed Fed officials weighing how they can respond to future troubles.

“A few” policymakers mulled boosting banks’ capital levels while some also said it is important to better prepare banks to use the Fed‘s emergency lending discount window facility, which is something officials have been working on for some time.

In addition, “a few” policymakers considered a novel strategy in which the Fed would set up a dedicated method of asset-buying that would explicitly target financial stability concerns.

The Fed is weighing the future of how it uses its balance sheet as a policy tool. Fed holdings have swollen massively over the last two decades due to huge bond purchases during the 2008 global financial crisis and the Covid-19 pandemic.

The pandemic experience has loomed particularly large because bond-buying that began in March 2020 started out as a stabilisation tool that morphed into outright stimulus.

Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack is among those who would like to see a more clearly defined system for buying bonds that would also entail a strategy to sell them when a crisis has passed.

Hammack said earlier this week that any programme “should also be temporary, and holdings should be sold in a timely way once market financial stability is restored.”

The minutes noted that “several” policymakers cautioned that monetary policy is not the right tool to deal with market trouble. But the large role now played by AI and technology investment in driving economic growth might complicate that view if large-scale problems emerged. REUTERS

data.title: Stocks to watch: SIA, Olam, F&N
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Tuesday (Nov 17):

Singapore Airlines (SIA) : The national carrier reported a 3.5 per cent rise in passenger traffic in October from the year-ago period amid “resilient” demand for air travel. SIA and its budget arm Scoot carried 3.7 million passengers during the month, up 4.5 per cent from a year ago. The group’s October passenger capacity concurrently rose 2.9 per cent, while the passenger load factor was up 0.5 percentage point at 87.8 per cent. Shares of SIA rose 0.8 per cent or S$0.06 to close at S$7.22 on Monday.

Olam : The agreement made by the agribusiness to sell its 32.4 per cent stake in port and logistics operator Arise P&L for US$175 million was terminated on Nov 15 as certain conditions of the deal were not fulfilled, it said in a bourse filing on Monday. Olam entered into a sale and purchase agreement with Dubai-based investment platform Equitane DMCC in April 2025 and expected the sale to close in FY2025. Shares of Olam ended Monday at S$0.845, down 1.7 per cent or S$0.015.

F&N : The beverage maker posted an 8.3 per cent year-on-year increase in net profit to S$63 million for the second half ended September, as its beverages business recovered and Vietnamese dairy associate Vinamilk contributed more to earnings. The board proposed a final dividend of S$0.04, unchanged from the previous year. Shares of F&N ended Monday flat at S$1.34.

data.title: Anthropic prices blockbuster IPO at US$83 a share: source
data.description:
ANTHROPIC priced its initial public offering at US$83 a share, above its targeted range of US$70 to US$78 per share on Wednesday (Nov 18), in one of the largest stock-market IPOs on record and the first by a major frontier artificial intelligence model developer, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The size of the offering has increased, the person said, asking not to be identified because the information isn’t public. Anthropic initially planned to sell 825 million shares.

Anthropic‘s sale is the second mega-IPO this year focused on AI, following June’s SpaceX sale, as investors jump at the chance for exposure to the fast-growing industry, even as the industry also faces mounting questions over the cost of developing and operating artificial intelligence models.

The AI lab comes to the public market just months after SpaceX’s record-setting IPO, even as the backdrop for AI stocks has turned more challenging.

Chipmakers and cloud companies central to the business have come under pressure in recent weeks due to valuation concerns, mounting AI infrastructure costs, and the sudden resignation of Jensen Huang as CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, a key pillar of the industry’s growth.

The pricing follows a roadshow that attracted demand several times the number of shares offered, Reuters previously reported, despite questions about the company’s outlook and its ability to sustain rapid growth as competition in the AI industry intensifies.

Anthropic‘s closest rival, OpenAI, is also expected to pursue a public listing as early as next year.

Anthropic declined to comment.

Bloomberg News first reported on the pricing.

Anthropic‘s growth has been driven by surging demand for its Claude models, particularly Claude Code, its coding agent that has gained popularity among software developers. Its annualised revenue run rate reached US$81 billion as of Oct 31, up US$10 billion from Sep 30, according to its IPO filing.

The Claude maker said it had 11,900 customers generating at least US$100,000 in annual revenue on a trailing 12-month basis as of Sep 30, compared with more than 1,500 at the end of last year, underscoring its growing business foothold.

But sustaining that growth is becoming expensive. Anthropic spent nearly US$9 billion on computing capacity and infrastructure in the first half of 2026, nearly four times the amount spent a year earlier. It also incurred an additional US$5 billion in computing costs in the third quarter, weighing on efficiency and reducing the revenue generated per dollar of computing capacity.

Revenue rose 47 per cent in the third quarter to US$16.96 billion. The company reported an operating loss of US$567 million, compared with operating income of US$974 million in the second quarter. Net ⁠loss fell ​to US$23.3 billion from US$66.3 billion a quarter earlier, including non-operating ​items related to bonds convertible into its shares.

Anthropic has committed to nearly US$900 billion in computing spending with infrastructure partners including Amazon and Alphabet’s Google, part of its ongoing expenditures to train and operate increasingly powerful AI models.

Its spending commitments also expose the company to risks beyond its own finances.

Anthropic warned in its prospectus that some of its computing providers and infrastructure partners depend on third-party financing and credit support to acquire chips and build capacity. “If such financing or support becomes unavailable or more costly, contracted capacity may be delayed, repriced, reduced, or not delivered,” Anthropic said in an IPO filing.

Investors have grown increasingly concerned about debt-fuelled expansion of AI infrastructure, with technology companies and data-centre operators borrowing heavily to finance chips, power and computing facilities.

Anthropic also faces questions over how it will balance its commercial ambitions with its emphasis on AI safety. CEO Dario Amodei has called for the industry to slow the pace of developing and releasing increasingly powerful models, warning that advances in AI could outstrip society’s ability to manage the risks.

Shares are expected to start trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT.

Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are the lead underwriters for Anthropic‘s offering, which has a 22-bank underwriting syndicate. The two banks also served as lead underwriters for SpaceX’s IPO earlier this year. REUTERS

data.title: Stocks to watch: Jardine Matheson, Riverstone, Deluge
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Wednesday (Nov 18):

Jardine Matheson: The Hong Kong-based conglomerate expects to post a 2026 dividend of at least US$2.50 per share, amid “strong performance” for the third quarter ended Sep 30. This comes after Jardine Matheson raised its full-year profit guidance in October to between US$5.50 and US$5.65 per share on an underlying basis, from the previous guidance of US$5.33 per share. For Q3, its Indonesian unit Astra International’s underlying net profit rose 11 per cent. Shares of Jardine Matheson closed 1 per cent or US$0.62 lower at US$59.15 on Tuesday, before the news.

Riverstone : The glove maker posted a 34.7 per cent rise in net profit to RM70.1 million (US$17.1 million) for the third quarter ended September. Riverstone’s Q3 revenue rose 27.3 per cent to RM315.1 million, marking the group’s highest quarterly revenue in over three years. It also announced that CEO Wong Teek Son will step down on Dec 1, to be succeeded by Chong Chu Mee. Riverstone shares closed 2.1 per cent or S$0.015 higher at S$0.745 on Tuesday, before the results.

Deluge : The fire detection and protection company has secured S$18.5 million in new contracts across Singapore and Malaysia, bringing its cumulative contract wins since January 2026 to more than S$147.7 million. The latest awards span infrastructure, marine and offshore, residential and industrial projects, including a Penang data centre project. Shares of Deluge closed 0.8 per cent or S$0.005 lower at S$0.605 on Tuesday.
